scenario_prompt: Write the response to this scored RFP question, worth 25% of the RFP's overall technical score: "Describe the migration approach and cutover plan." Context: the migration moves load-matching and carrier-settlement systems off on-premises Microsoft SQL Server (28 instances, 620 Hyper-V virtual machines) onto Google Cloud (Google Compute Engine for compute, Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL for the data layer), within a 2-year, $4,200,000 programme, with proposals due 2026-11-15 and the buyer's next compliance audit opening in 6 months. Return only the answer text, no section headers beyond what the answer itself needs.
text:
Our approach treats this as two migrations with different risk profiles running under one programme. Load-matching is latency-sensitive but replayable — a bad minute costs matches, not money. Carrier settlement is financially material, audit-scoped, and must be reconcilable to the cent. We sequence, cut over, and roll back the two differently, and we say so explicitly rather than applying one pattern to both.

**Phase 0 — Assess and land (months 1–4).** We begin with automated discovery across the 620 Hyper-V virtual machines and 28 SQL Server instances using Migration Center and agent-based dependency mapping, producing a signed-off application-to-VM-to-database dependency graph before any workload moves. In parallel we run schema and code assessment of every SQL Server database, because the SQL Server–to–Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL step is heterogeneous: collation and case-sensitivity semantics, `IDENTITY` and sequence behaviour, `MERGE`, T-SQL stored procedures and triggers, CLR assemblies, SQL Agent jobs, linked servers, and any Service Broker or MSDTC-coordinated distributed transaction all require conversion or redesign. We classify every object as auto-convertible, convertible-with-review, or requiring re-engineering, and we price the third category into the plan rather than discovering it mid-cutover. Concurrently we build the landing zone — organisation hierarchy, VPC and interconnect, IAM and CMEK key management, Cloud Logging and Cloud Audit Logs retention, backup and DR policy — as infrastructure-as-code.

**Compliance audit alignment.** Your next audit opens roughly six months from award. We treat that as a hard constraint on the plan, not a background risk. Our commitment is that no settlement workload is mid-flight when the audit window opens. By the audit date we will have delivered the landing zone with evidence artifacts already in place — control mappings, key management and access-review records, immutable audit log export, and the segregation-of-duties model for the migration tooling itself — plus one or two low-criticality non-settlement workloads migrated end-to-end as a demonstrable, auditable reference implementation. Settlement databases remain on the existing estate and under existing controls through the audit. This gives the auditor a completed, documented control environment to examine rather than a half-migrated data layer, and it gives your team a defensible answer to the "who can touch production data during migration" question. We institute a change freeze covering the two weeks either side of the audit opening.

**Phase 1 — Compute migration (months 4–14).** The 620 virtual machines move in waves grouped by the dependency graph, not by convenience. Each wave is a complete application slice — all tiers of a service move together — sized at roughly 40–60 VMs, which puts a wave every three to four weeks with buffer. Where Migrate to Virtual Machines supports the source hypervisor and guest OS, we use agent-based replication with test-clone capability; for Hyper-V guests and legacy operating systems outside that support matrix we use image import or rebuild-from-configuration-management, and we identify which VMs fall into each category during Phase 0 rather than assuming lift-and-shift applies uniformly. Every wave runs at least one non-disruptive test clone in an isolated VPC before the production cut. VMs whose only purpose is hosting SQL Server are not migrated — they are decommissioned when the corresponding database lands on Cloud SQL, which is a material part of how this programme pays for itself.

**Phase 2 — Data layer (months 8–20, overlapping compute).** For each of the 28 instances: convert schema, convert procedural code, then establish continuous change-data-capture replication from the on-premises SQL Server into Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Replication runs for a minimum of two weeks before any cutover, during which we operate the target in shadow mode — production traffic is mirrored read-only against the target, and we compare results row-by-row and query-by-query. We run automated reconciliation continuously: row counts, checksums on financially material tables, and full recomputation of settlement balances on both platforms with a zero-variance gate. A database does not become a cutover candidate until it has held zero variance for seven consecutive days at full production volume.

**Cutover mechanics.** Load-matching cuts over blue/green. Both platforms run live; we shift traffic progressively — 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% — with automatic rollback triggered on match-rate deviation, p99 latency regression, or error-rate threshold breach. Reverse replication from Cloud SQL back to SQL Server runs throughout the shift, so rollback at any percentage is a traffic-routing change measured in minutes, with no data loss.

Carrier settlement cuts over differently, because progressive traffic splitting across a financial ledger creates split-brain risk we will not accept. We use a quiesced cut inside a scheduled settlement window: drain in-flight batches, confirm zero open transactions, allow replication to reach zero lag, freeze the source read-only, run the final reconciliation gate, then repoint. Target window is four to six hours against a maintenance window we agree with you and with affected carriers. We hold the source in read-only standby with reverse replication active for a full settlement cycle after the cut — no source decommissioning until at least one complete settlement run has executed on Cloud SQL and been reconciled and signed off by your finance team. Rollback during this period is a repoint back to the preserved source.

Each cutover has a named go/no-go decision point, pre-agreed rollback triggers with numeric thresholds, a rollback rehearsal completed in the test clone, and a designated decision owner from your side who holds the abort authority. We rehearse the settlement rollback at least once against real production-scale data before the live cut.

**Phase 3 — Optimise and decommission (months 18–24).** Rightsizing against observed Cloud Monitoring data, committed-use discount purchase once consumption has stabilised, high-availability and read-replica topology finalisation, disaster-recovery failover test, and staged decommissioning of the Hyper-V estate and SQL Server licences. Licence retirement is deliberately back-loaded — we do not book the saving until the source is genuinely redundant.

**Where the $4,200,000 goes and what we will tell you plainly.** Roughly 55% is migration engineering labour, weighted toward the data layer because heterogeneous database conversion, not VM movement, is where this programme's real cost and real risk sit. Roughly 20% is Google Cloud consumption during the parallel-run period, when you are paying for both estates simultaneously — this overlap is unavoidable and we have budgeted it rather than hiding it. The balance covers testing and reconciliation tooling, landing zone and security engineering, contingency, and knowledge transfer. The largest single uncertainty in the plan is the volume of settlement stored-procedure logic that requires re-engineering rather than mechanical conversion; Phase 0 exists to convert that unknown into a number within the first four months, and we will bring you a re-baselined plan at that gate if the assessment warrants it.
